Have things improved since? On the contrary, I feel like we’re slipping down a well-oiled slope with no end in sight. Vulnerabilities are reported at unprecedented rates. A lot of people are doing everything they can to patch them up, which doesn’t necessarily mean they’re not making things even worse. Complex software involves complex trees of dependencies, and every branch on that tree needs tending to. When they stop being reliable, people further down the tree start taking more weight. And there’s a limit of how much a single person can do, so what started as an effort to resolve an issue upstream may quickly become a weakness. Is software less secure these days? It’s tempting to say yes. I’d love to blame the corporate sector for egotistically dumping low quality software on us. I’d love to blame marketing-oriented people developing stuff with the sole goal of making a profit. I’d love to blame Rust for getting people obsessed about memory safety, and ignoring the kinds of vulnerabilities that aren’t caught by the compiler. Finally, I’d really love to blame slop. But the truth is, I don’t know. That’s really beside the point. The point is that nowadays everyone and their chatbot became security researchers. Projects are being flooded with vulnerability reports. Even though pretty much every bug bounty was discontinued because of slop, people aren’t stopping. And even if we disregard truly invalid junk reports, there’s a lot left, and you have to deal with them somehow. page.text_excerpt: micjm blog about subscribe Yes, 17m lines of Lean is a lot 2026-11-22 The recent proof of the Riemann hypothesis came with a statistic attached: the proof is 17 million lines of Lean. Beyond the philosophical questions of what it means to have a proof longer than any human could comprehend, I’m left with a simpler question: is that as large as it sounds? To investigate, I hunted for collections of Lean proofs online. I found two and charted the lengths of their proofs. (All charts have a log x axis, which makes 17m lines look a lot closer to 1m and 100k than it really is.) Famous theorems in Mathlib Mathlib maintains a collection of famous proofs. There are over 1k but only 259 have Lean associated, which I chart here. These are all human generated, and as we can see, they come nowhere close to 17m. Every Lean package on Reservoir Reservoir indexes every published Lean package, 938 of which have Lean code on GitHub. This one has a lot more data, including AI assisted proofs. We even have a few that are over 16m!: 88m: Qiuzhen-CFSG/CFSG this appears to be an AI built proof that is still a work in progress. 36m: CBirkbeck/LeanBridge, a project linking the LMFDB database of number theory objects to Mathlib. This isn’t really a proof: about 98% of its Lean is files generated by scripts that check the database’s numbers one by one. The hand-written part is closer to 500k lines. 27m: anthropics/fermats-last-theorem is another Anthropic special: a complete proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem, published on GitHub in September. Its README says “the Lean sources were produced by AI agents building on human-written open-source Lean”, including the human FLT project led by Kevin Buzzard, which is about 60k lines and still in progress. If you do not write for other people, stop reading this now. When I was at Snowflake, one of the coolest things that everybody did was this etiquette thing. The first sentence of each email would be “If you don’t develop in this specific part of the code, you can stop reading.” or “If you’re not part of the finance org, you can stop reading.” This made me think a lot about what it means to write for other people. You need to be subservient to your audience. Similarly, thinking about how much space you take is very important. For Slack/Teams threads, you would start with a 3- to 5-line introduction to your topic, and then people could find more details inside the threads. My Time Pi is connected to an outside GNSS antenna through a TimeHAT v6, which I paired with a high quality timing-grade GNSS module, the u-blox ZED-F9T. I posted a video about the setup today on YouTube: I'd encourage anyone else interested in network time to contribute to the NTP Pool. However, there are some things you should know before contributing your own time services: Time Commitment You don't need to go all out with a timing-grade GNSS module like I'm using. Heck, you don't even need GNSS-backed time at all! The main requirements for hosting a node in the global NTP pool are: Keeping the system online (servers are only made active in the pool if they're online and serving good time consistently for a long period) Maintaining a good time—which can mean Stratum 1 GNSS service, but could also mean pulling time from a few other reliable time servers, and running as Stratum 2 or 3 A stable IP address (IPv4 and/or IPv6), and a long-term commitment Just 'testing the waters' in the Pool wastes resources—when you bring a new server online, it will take at least a few hours just to spin up all the tests to verify the server's providing a good time. If you just want to operate your own time server, that's fine; the NTP Pool is a shared global resource, so joining it is a little more of a commitment. The concept of a unit in unit test is not really defined, integration tests are integrating arbitrarily scoped modules, the concept of an E2E test makes sense, but it very much underspecifies the actually tested behavior as well as methods for testing it, are you using automated agents, human supervision, predefined set of actions, random exploration... it's all sweeped under the rug. On the other side you have your stress tests, load tests, peneration tests etc. but there is no proper classification in the wild, it all seems to be based on "vibes". Sounds familiar? I bet it does. I encountered issues like this so many times I'm afraid to count. But recently AWS released a new tool called Emulator that emulates actual AWS API endpoints. Defining the problem # The problem with the difference between plan and apply jobs is that plan can't possibly emulate every actual API call against a live infrastructure. These mock calls can't know for a fact that you already have a resource in AWS called "my-bucket-asdasdasd" or that you're trying to upgrade a PostgreSQL RDS instance from version 14 to version 18 without an explicit "apply immediately" flag. There are multiple tools that can emulate AWS services either partially or in full, but what they lack is the actual knowledge of the service architecture. page.text_excerpt: Skip to main content Go to the 9to5Mac home page Switch site Toggle social menu Toggle dark mode Toggle search form Forums Store Podcasts iPhone Mac iPad Watch Vision Music and TV Guides MAC MACOS MACOS 27 MACOS 27.3 How to hide the new macOS 27.3 menu bar indicator Zac Hall | Nov 17 2026 - 7:02 am PT 0 Comments macOS 27.3 beta 2 adds a blue menu bar indicator for apps using System & App Protection Override. Apple describes it as a transparency indicator that appears when one app is controlling another. If you regularly use trusted automation tools and utilities, that can mean a persistent pill taking up space in your menu bar. Prefer to hide it? There’s a Terminal workaround. I’ve tested this on macOS 27.3 beta 2 and confirmed that the indicator disappears after a restart. Open Terminal and run these two commands: sudo mkdir -p /Library/Preferences/FeatureFlags/Domain sudo defaults write /Library/Preferences/FeatureFlags/Domain/TCC AX_TRANSPARENCY_INDICATOR -dict Enabled -bool false Enter your Mac administrator password when prompted, then restart your Mac. The command disables the internal AX_TRANSPARENCY_INDICATOR feature flag. It doesn’t remove apps from your permissions list, although you’ll no longer see this activity indicator. To restore Apple’s default behavior, run: sudo defaults delete /Library/Preferences/FeatureFlags/Domain/TCC AX_TRANSPARENCY_INDICATOR Restart your Mac again to apply the reversal. This removes only the indicator override, preserving any other flags you may have configured. This is an undocumented workaround tested on the current beta, so Apple could change or remove it in a future update. Not a fan of this on macOS 27.3 beta 2. page.text_excerpt: arv-o-matic The Weblog of Erik Arvidsson Multithreaded JavaScript « Revival Multithreaded JavaScript 2 Nov 2026 | JavaScriptTypeScriptWebAssemblyOpen Source Over the last few weeks I haven't been able to stop thinking about multithreaded JavaScript. It all started with me seeing Jarred Sumner's PR adding shared-memory threads to JavaScriptCore in Bun's fork of WebKit. It pointed to Filip Pizlo's WebKit blog post "Concurrent JavaScript: It can work!". The idea behind both is to allow multiple threads that share the same memory. The threads share the same realm (global) and module graph. This is different from Workers where each worker has its own heap (memory), global and module graph. With a shared heap, reading and writing the same JavaScript object from different threads becomes possible. const o = {value: 1}; const t = new Thread(() => { console.log(o.value); // 1 o.value = 2; }); console.log(o.value); // 1 or 2 await t.asyncJoin(); console.log(o.value); // 2 What Pizlo's blog post outlines is how to make this cheap. Reads never lock, no matter which thread does them. Every object remembers the thread that created it, and that thread gets to write to it after a single compare of a lock word. Only when another thread wants to write does the object get handed over and become locked. Races are allowed. A racing read may see any interleaving, but it never crashes, never sees a torn or made-up value, and a write to an unrelated property is never lost. So I built it. Three times, in fact, each time giving up a bit of the model to get something that runs today. Describe the companies or people you want. Enrichable finds them, then researches every row with AI and live web data. Start enriching View on GitHub Free and open source (MIT) Powered by Context.dev What is Enrichable? Enrichable is a free, open-source AI spreadsheet for data enrichment. You describe the list you need, such as “every solar company in the US with 50+ employees”, and it fills a sheet with matching companies or people. Then you add columns by asking questions in plain English. Enrichable answers each one for every row by searching the web, reading pages and pulling company and contact data. Every answer keeps its sources, so you can check the work before you use it. What you can do with it Build lead lists from a prompt Ask for “every Series A fintech in Europe” or “VPs of Sales at US logistics companies”. Matching companies or people stream into the sheet, deduplicated by domain. Research every row Add a column with a question like “Who is the CEO?” or “Does the pricing page offer a free tier?”. Enrichable answers it for each row and links every answer to its sources. Qualify and score accounts True or false checks, categories and scores on levels you define. Each call comes with a probability or confidence, so you can filter on how sure it is. Find work emails One column tries your email providers in order (Hunter, Prospeo, Apollo, QuickEnrich, ContactOut) and keeps the first work email it finds. Draft outreach and documents Write a personalized email or a branded PDF for every row, using the research already in the sheet. page.description: It’s time to rethink welfare as AI reshapes the economy and wears down the brains of some of the most vulnerable workers

We need to rethink welfare for an economy being reshaped by AI. Throughout the history of the study of economics, the human brain, which directs our labour, judgment and resilience, has rarely been considered an asset in its own right. The emerging AI economy is changing that. As machines take on routine work, what becomes most valuable is the judgment, creativity and insights only people can provide. Economists coined a term for this in recent years: brain capital. The World Economic Forum finds analytical thinking is now the skill employers value most, and estimates that 59 in every 100 workers will need training to adapt to this shift by 2030. In September, I found myself at the first Global Brain Economy Summit in New York asking a hard question: how much room is there for creativity and learning when one’s mind is consumed by anxieties about paying rent or for food to last through the week?
